proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal P_n\).  By the definitions of threshold assignment and observed treatment, the right and left limits of the treatment regression are, respectively,
\[
 \mu^+_{D,P}(c_P)=E_P[D(1)\mid X=c_P],\qquad
 \mu^-_{D,P}(c_P)=E_P[D(0)\mid X=c_P].
\]
Here the equalities at \(c_P\) use the continuous versions supplied by assumption ass:potential-reduced-form-continuity.  The response-type definition gives the pointwise identity
\[
 D(1)-D(0)=\mathbf 1\{R=C\}.
\]
Subtracting the two preceding conditional expectations therefore yields
\[
 d_P=E_P[D(1)-D(0)\mid X=c_P]=P(R=C\mid X=c_P).
\]
Likewise, consistency and exclusion are encoded by \(Y=Y(D)\): immediately to the right of the cutoff the observed potential response is \(Y(D(1))\), and immediately to the left it is \(Y(D(0))\).  Hence continuity of the potential reduced forms gives
\[
 y_P=E_P[Y(D(1))-Y(D(0))\mid X=c_P].
\]
For never-takers and always-takers, \(D(1)=D(0)\), whereas for compliers \((D(0),D(1))=(0,1)\).  Consequently, pointwise,
\[
 Y(D(1))-Y(D(0))=(Y(1)-Y(0))\mathbf 1\{R=C\},
\]
and thus
\[
 y_P=E_P[(Y(1)-Y(0))\mathbf 1\{R=C\}\mid X=c_P].
\]
Assumption ass:local-compliance-strength gives \(d_P\ge\kappa_n>0\), so division is valid.  Dividing the last display by the formula for \(d_P\) proves
\[
 \theta_P=\frac{y_P}{d_P}=E_P[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid R=C,X=c_P].
\]

Write \(a=a_\star=1/256\).  Since \(h_n\le1/32\), one has \((16h_n)^{-1}\ge2\), and hence \(J_n=\lfloor(16h_n)^{-1}\rfloor\ge2\).  The four entries of the common table are
\[
 q_{00}=q_{11}=\frac38,\qquad q_{01}=\frac{1/4+g_\star}{2},\qquad q_{10}=\frac{1/4-g_\star}{2}.
\]
Because \(|g_\star|\le a\), they sum to one and satisfy
\[
 \frac{63}{512}=\frac{1/4-a}{2}\le q_{u_0,u_1}(x)\le\frac38.
\]

For \(B(t)=1-10t^3+15t^4-6t^5\), direct differentiation gives
\[
 B'(t)=-30t^2(1-t)^2,\qquad B''(t)=-60t+180t^2-120t^3.
\]
On \([0,1]\), \(\lVert B'\rVert_\infty\le15/8\) and \(\lVert B''\rVert_\infty\le15\).  The first derivative of the middle piece of \(g_\star\) is \(8aB'(4x-3/2)\), and this derivative vanishes at both junctions.  It follows that
\[
 \lVert g_\star'\rVert_\infty\le15a,\qquad
 \operatorname{Lip}(g_\star')\le480a.
\]
For \(\beta=s-1\in(0,1]\), a Lipschitz function on an interval of diameter one has \(\beta\)-H\"older seminorm no larger than its Lipschitz constant; hence \([g_\star']_{s-1}\le480a\).  This proves the asserted bounds for \(q_{u_0,u_1}\), including
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}(q_{u_0,u_1})\le\frac{15a}{2},\qquad
 \lVert q_{u_0,u_1}'\rVert_\infty\le\frac{15a}{2},\qquad
 [q_{u_0,u_1}']_{s-1}\le240a
\]
in the respective regimes.

On \((-1,1)\), direct differentiation of the quartic profile gives
\[
 \psi'(u)=-4u(1-u^2),\qquad \psi''(u)=-4+12u^2.
\]
Both \(\psi\) and \(\psi'\) join continuously to zero at the support boundary.  Therefore
\[
 \lVert\psi'\rVert_\infty\le2,\qquad \operatorname{Lip}(\psi')\le8,\qquad [\psi']_{s-1}\le8.
\]
For \(w=w_{j,\ell}\), scaling gives, when \(s=1\),
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}(w)\le \frac{2\kappa_n}{h_n}=\frac{M}{16}.
\]
When \(1<s\le2\), the identity \(h_n^s=32\kappa_n/M\), together with \(h_n\le1\), gives
\[
 \lVert w'\rVert_\infty\le\frac{2\kappa_n}{h_n}
 =\frac{M}{16}h_n^{s-1}\le\frac{M}{16},
 \qquad [w']_{s-1}\le\frac{8\kappa_n}{h_n^s}=\frac{M}{4}.
\]

The location formula and \(j\le J_n\le(16h_n)^{-1}\) imply
\[
 \operatorname{supp}(w_{j,+})=[c_{j,+}-h_n,c_{j,+}+h_n]\subset[1/4,3/8]
\]
and
\[
 \operatorname{supp}(w_{j,-})\subset[5/8,3/4].
\]
Adjacent supports can meet only at an endpoint, and nonadjacent or oppositely labelled supports are disjoint.  Thus distinct profiles have product zero almost everywhere.  On each such support \(g_\star\), and hence every entry of \(q\), is constant.  Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}(wq_{u_0,u_1})\le\frac{3M}{128}
\]
when \(s=1\), while for \(1<s\le2\),
\[
 \lVert(wq_{u_0,u_1})'\rVert_\infty\le\frac{3M}{128},
 \qquad [(wq_{u_0,u_1})']_{s-1}\le\frac{3M}{32}.
\]
These are the claimed complier-cell bounds, since \(0\le wq_{u_0,u_1}\le3\kappa_n/8\).

For an always-taker or never-taker cell, put \(f=(1-w)q_{u_0,u_1}/2\).  On the transition region \((3/8,5/8)\), \(w=0\), while on the support of \(w\), \(q_{u_0,u_1}\) is constant.  Splitting at the junctions therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}(f)\le\frac{15a}{4}+\frac{3M}{256}
\]
for \(s=1\), and
\[
 \lVert f'\rVert_\infty\le\frac{15a}{4}+\frac{3M}{256},\qquad
 [f']_{s-1}\le120a+\frac{3M}{64}
\]
for \(1<s\le2\).  For the last inequality, within the middle transition the seminorm is at most \(120a\), within the bump it is at most \((3/16)(M/4)=3M/64\), and for points in different regions the derivative vanishes at the intervening junction, so the two bounds add.  Since \(M\ge2\) and \(a=1/256\), all displayed function, derivative, and seminorm bounds are at most \(M\).  Also \(0\le w\le\kappa_n\le1/8\), so all twelve latent masses are nonnegative, their sum is
\[
 \sum_{u_0,u_1}q_{u_0,u_1}\left(w+\frac{1-w}{2}+\frac{1-w}{2}\right)=1,
\]
and the stated upper bounds follow.  This proves all latent and common-table H\"older claims.

Conditional on \(X=x\), the potential-outcome table is the same for all response types.  Thus assignment below and above the cutoff gives
\[
 \mu^-_{D,P_{j,\ell}}=\frac{1-w}{2},\qquad
 \mu^+_{D,P_{j,\ell}}=\frac{1+w}{2}.
\]
The table also gives
\[
 E[Y(0)\mid X=x]=\frac{1-g_\star(x)}2,\qquad
 E[Y(1)\mid X=x]=\frac{1+g_\star(x)}2.
\]
Combining these identities with the treatment probabilities yields
\[
 \mu^-_{Y,P_{j,\ell}}=\frac12-\frac{g_\star w}{2},\qquad
 \mu^+_{Y,P_{j,\ell}}=\frac12+\frac{g_\star w}{2}.
\]
On the support of \(w\), \(g_\star\) equals either \(a\) or \(-a\).  The preceding scaling bounds therefore give Lipschitz constants \(M/32\) and \(aM/32\) for the nonconstant treatment and outcome parts when \(s=1\), and derivative suprema of the same sizes and derivative H\"older seminorms \(M/8\) and \(aM/8\) when \(1<s\le2\).  As the constant parts lie in \([0,1]\) and \(M\ge2\), all four extensions are in the required radius-\(M\) ball.

The functions just displayed are continuous, so the potential reduced forms are continuous at the cutoff.  Since \(w(c_{j,\ell})=\kappa_n\),
\[
 d_{P_{j,\ell}}=\kappa_n,\qquad
 y_{P_{j,\ell}}=g_\star(c_{j,\ell})\kappa_n.
\]
The support inclusions place \(c_{j,+}\) on the \(+a\) plateau and \(c_{j,-}\) on the \(-a\) plateau.  Division by \(d_{P_{j,\ell}}>0\) gives \(\theta_{P_{j,+}}=a\) and \(\theta_{P_{j,-}}=-a\).

The response-type weights factor from the common potential-outcome table.  Hence, for every observable cell,
\[
 p^{D,Y}_{j,\ell}(x,d,y)=p^D_{j,\ell}(x,d)m_{d,y}(x).
\]
Here \(p^D_{j,\ell}(x,d)\ge(1-\kappa_n)/2\), while the table gives \(m_{d,y}(x)\ge(1-a)/2\).  Therefore
\[
 p^{D,Y}_{j,\ell}(x,d,y)\ge\frac{(1-\kappa_n)(1-a)}4>\frac1{64}>v.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 E[Y\mid D,X=x]=\frac12+g_\star(x)\left(D-\frac12\right).
\]
Conditional variance decomposition and conditional covariance decomposition now give, on either observable side,
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)=\frac{1-g_\star(x)^2}{4}
       +g_\star(x)^2\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x),
\]
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(Y,D\mid X=x)=g_\star(x)\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x).
\]
The first expression is at least \((1-a^2)/4>v\).  If the treatment variance is positive, using \(\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x)\le1/4\) in the ratio gives
\[
 \frac{|\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D\mid X=x)|}
 {\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x)}}
 \le\frac{a}{\sqrt{1-a^2}}<1-v.
\]
If it is zero, the covariance identity makes the covariance zero.  All remaining class conditions were already verified, so \(\mathcal W_n\subset\mathcal P_n\).

Under \(R_\star\), the conditional law of \(Y\) given \((X,D)\) is the same margin \(m_{d,y}\).  Cancelling it in the density ratio gives, outside the null set \(X=c_{j,\ell}\),
\[
 \frac{dP_{j,\ell}}{dR_\star}
 =1+(2D-1)\operatorname{sgn}(X-c_{j,\ell})w_{j,\ell}(X).
\]
Thus the one-sample and product likelihood ratios are measurable with respect to the treatment and running-variable observations alone.  Direct polynomial integration gives
\[
 \int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)^4\,du
 =2\left(1-\frac43+\frac65-\frac47+\frac19\right)=\frac{256}{315}.
\]
If two indices are distinct, conditioning on \(X\) and averaging \(2D-1\) under the fair treatment law \(R_\star\) gives an inner product equal to one plus the integral of the product of their signed profiles; that product is zero almost everywhere.  For one index, the same calculation and the last integral give
\[
 E_{R_\star}\left[\left(\frac{dP_{j,\ell}}{dR_\star}\right)^2\right]
 =1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n.
\]
Independence raises this inner product to the \(n\)-th power.  Expanding the square of the equally weighted mixture likelihood ratio, with \(J_n\) diagonal terms and \(J_n(J_n-1)\) off-diagonal terms, proves
\[
 \chi^2(Q_{\ell,n},R_\star^{\otimes n})
 =\frac{\left(1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}.
\]

Put \(c=c_P\), which is supplied to the oracle rule.  We first construct an explicit uniformly honest rule.  Let
\[
 K(u)=(4-6u)\mathbf 1\{0\le u\le1\}.
\]
Then \(\int_0^1K(u)\,du=1\), \(\int_0^1uK(u)\,du=0\), and \(B_K=\int_0^1K(u)^2\,du<\infty\).  Set \(h=n^{-1/(2s+1)}\).  For \(V\in\{D,Y\}\), define the sample maps
\[
 \widehat\mu_V^+=\frac1{nh}\sum_{i=1}^nK\left(\frac{X_i-c}{h}\right)
 \mathbf 1\{c\le X_i\le c+h\}V_i,
\]
\[
 \widehat\mu_V^-=\frac1{nh}\sum_{i=1}^nK\left(\frac{c-X_i}{h}\right)
 \mathbf 1\{c-h\le X_i<c\}V_i.
\]
For all sufficiently large \(n\), assumption ass:interior-cutoff ensures that both windows lie in \([0,1]\).  Uniformity of \(X\) and a change of variables show that their expectations are the corresponding integrals of \(K(u)\mu^\ell_{V,P}(c\pm hu)\).

For \(s=1\), the H\"older condition directly bounds the bias by
\[
 M h\int_0^1|K(u)|u\,du.
\]
For \(1<s\le2\), write \(\beta=s-1\).  The fundamental theorem of calculus and the derivative H\"older bound give
\[
 |f(c+t)-f(c)-tf'(c)|
 \le\int_0^{|t|}M r^\beta\,dr
 =\frac{M}{s}|t|^s.
\]
The zero first moment of \(K\) cancels the linear term, giving the same order \(C_KMh^s\).  Since \(0\le V_i\le1\), independence and the uniform design give
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_P(\widehat\mu_V^\ell)\le\frac{B_K}{nh}.
\]
For any centered random variable \(U\), the pointwise inequality \(\mathbf 1\{|U|>t\}\le U^2/t^2\) implies \(P(|U|>t)\le E[U^2]/t^2\).  Applying this inequality to the four estimators and taking a union bound, there is a constant \(C=C(s,M,\alpha)\) such that, with probability at least \(1-\alpha\), all four errors are at most \(C\rho_n/2\).  Thus, for
\[
 \widehat d=\widehat\mu_D^+-\widehat\mu_D^-,\qquad
 \widehat y=\widehat\mu_Y^+-\widehat\mu_Y^-,\qquad r_n=C\rho_n,
\]
the event
\[
 \mathcal E_P=\{|\widehat d-d_P|\le r_n,\ |\widehat y-y_P|\le r_n\}
\]
has probability at least \(1-\alpha\), uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_n\).

If \(\kappa_n\le2r_n\), define the oracle interval to be \(\Theta\).  Otherwise put
\[
 \widetilde d=\max\{\widehat d,\kappa_n/2\},\qquad
 \widetilde\theta=\Pi_\Theta(\widehat y/\widetilde d),
\]
where \(\Pi_\Theta\) is metric projection onto \([-1,1]\), and define
\[
 I_n^{\mathrm{known}}=
 \Theta\cap[\widetilde\theta-4r_n/\kappa_n,
              \widetilde\theta+4r_n/\kappa_n].
\]
This is a measurable connected interval.  On \(\mathcal E_P\) in the second regime, \(\widehat d\ge d_P-r_n>\kappa_n/2\), so \(\widetilde d=\widehat d\).  Since \(|y_P|=|\theta_P|d_P\le d_P\),
\[
 \left|\frac{\widehat y}{\widehat d}-\frac{y_P}{d_P}\right|
 \le\frac{|\widehat y-y_P|}{\widehat d}
 +\frac{|y_P|\,|\widehat d-d_P|}{d_P\widehat d}
 \le\frac{2r_n}{\widehat d}\le\frac{4r_n}{\kappa_n}.
\]
Projection cannot increase distance from \(\theta_P\in\Theta\), so the interval covers \(\theta_P\) on \(\mathcal E_P\).  It is therefore uniformly \((1-\alpha)\)-honest.  Its length is deterministically at most \(8r_n/\kappa_n\) in the second regime and is two in the first.  Because \(r_n=C\rho_n\), enlarging a constant if necessary gives
\[
 L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\le C_0\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}.
\]

For the converse, it is enough to exhibit two laws in the same class with the supplied cutoff \(c=1/2\).  Let
\[
 \varphi(u)=(1-u^2)^2\mathbf 1\{|u|\le1\},\quad
 a_n=\eta\min\{\kappa_n,\rho_n\},\quad
 \delta_n=a_n/\kappa_n,\quad
 h_a=(8a_n/M)^{1/s},
\]
where \(\eta\in(0,1/8]\) will be fixed below.  Under both laws, take \(X\) uniform and, conditionally on \(X\), assign response-type probabilities
\[
 P(R=C)=\kappa_n,\qquad P(R=N)=P(R=A)=\frac{1-\kappa_n}{2}.
\]
For never-takers and always-takers let the four potential-outcome cells each have probability \(1/4\).  Under \(P_t\), \(t\in\{0,1\}\), give compliers the table
\[
 q_{00,t}=q_{11,t}=\frac38,\qquad
 q_{01,t}(x)=\frac{1/4+g_t(x)}2,\qquad
 q_{10,t}(x)=\frac{1/4-g_t(x)}2,\qquad
 g_t(x)=t\delta_n\varphi\left(\frac{x-c}{h_a}\right).
\]
For large \(n\), \(h_a<1/4\); all cells are nonnegative because \(\delta_n\le\eta\le1/8\).  Both laws have
\[
 \mu_D^-=(1-\kappa_n)/2,\qquad \mu_D^+=(1+\kappa_n)/2,
\]
and their outcome extensions are
\[
 \mu_{Y,P_t}^-(x)=\frac12-\frac{\kappa_ng_t(x)}2,\qquad
 \mu_{Y,P_t}^+(x)=\frac12+\frac{\kappa_ng_t(x)}2.
\]
The derivative calculations \(\lVert\varphi'\rVert_\infty\le2\) and \([\varphi']_{s-1}\le8\), together with \(h_a^s=8a_n/M\), show that the nonconstant outcome parts have Lipschitz constant at most \(M/8\) for \(s=1\), and derivative supremum at most \(M/8\) and derivative H\"older seminorm at most \(M/2\) for \(1<s\le2\).  Thus the observable extensions lie in the radius-\(M\) H\"older ball.  The corresponding potential reduced forms are the same continuous functions, so the causal continuity condition holds.  At the cutoff,
\[
 d_{P_t}=\kappa_n,\qquad \theta_{P_0}=0,\qquad \theta_{P_1}=\delta_n.
\]

For completeness, the binary outcome has mean \(1/2\mp\kappa_ng_t/2\) on the two sides, so
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_t}(Y\mid X=x)=\frac14-\frac{\kappa_n^2g_t(x)^2}{4}>\frac{63}{256}>v.
\]
Also \(\operatorname{Var}(D\mid X=x)=(1-\kappa_n^2)/4\ge63/256\), and a direct two-point covariance calculation on either side gives
\[
 |\operatorname{Cov}(Y,D\mid X=x)|=\frac{\kappa_n|g_t(x)|(1-\kappa_n)}4\le\frac1{256}.
\]
The resulting absolute correlation is at most \(1/63<63/64<1-v\).  Thus \(P_0,P_1\in\mathcal P_n\).

Under \(P_0\), each outcome cell within a treatment stratum is equiprobable.  On the left, passing to \(P_1\) changes only the two \(D=0\) cells by \(\pm\kappa_ng_1(x)/2\); on the right it changes only the two \(D=1\) cells by those amounts.  Since the relevant baseline cell probability is \((1+\kappa_n)/4\), the conditional chi-square divergence is at most \(2\kappa_n^2g_1(x)^2\).  Therefore, with \(C_\varphi=\int_{-1}^1\varphi(u)^2\,du=256/315\),
\[
 \chi^2(P_1,P_0)\le2C_\varphi a_n^2h_a.
\]
Product expansion and \(1+x\le e^x\) yield
\[
 \chi^2(P_1^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 \le\exp\left\{2C_\varphi n a_n^2(8a_n/M)^{1/s}\right\}-1.
\]
Since \(n\rho_n^{2+1/s}=1\), the exponent is at most a constant times \(\eta^{2+1/s}\).  Choose \(\eta=\eta(s,M,\alpha)>0\) small enough that the last display is at most \((1-2\alpha)^2\).  Writing \(L=dP_1^{\otimes n}/dP_0^{\otimes n}\), the total-variation identity and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_1^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})
 =\frac12E_{P_0^{\otimes n}}|L-1|
 \le\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(P_1^{\otimes n},P_0^{\otimes n})}
 \le\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
\]
If an oracle interval is honest under both laws, then under \(P_0\) the probability that it contains both \(0\) and \(\delta_n\) is at least
\[
 1-2\alpha-\operatorname{TV}(P_0^{\otimes n},P_1^{\otimes n})
 \ge\frac{1-2\alpha}{2}.
\]
Connectedness forces its length to be at least \(\delta_n\) on that event.  Hence
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P[|I_n^{\mathrm{known}}|]
 \ge\frac{\eta(1-2\alpha)}2\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}.
\]
Taking the infimum over honest oracle rules proves the lower bound and completes the theorem.

Let \(I_n\) be any interval rule satisfying the honesty condition in def:minimax-length.  Every component of \(Q_{+,n}\) belongs to \(\mathcal P_n\) and has effect label \(a_\star\), whereas every component of \(Q_{-,n}\) belongs to \(\mathcal P_n\) and has label \(-a_\star\), by prop:outcome-invariant-witness.  Averaging the componentwise coverage inequalities gives
\[
 Q_{+,n}\{a_\star\in I_n\}\ge1-\alpha,\qquad
 Q_{-,n}\{-a_\star\in I_n\}\ge1-\alpha.
\]
For probability measures \(Q\ll R\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(Q,R)
 =\frac12E_R\left|\frac{dQ}{dR}-1\right|
 \le\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(Q,R)}.
\]
The triangle inequality for total variation and the equal chi-square formulas for the two labels therefore imply
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(Q_{+,n},Q_{-,n})
 \le\sqrt{\frac{\left(1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}}.
\]
Transferring the second coverage event from \(Q_{-,n}\) to \(Q_{+,n}\), and then using the union bound under \(Q_{+,n}\), yields
\[
 Q_{+,n}\{-a_\star,a_\star\in I_n\}
 \ge1-2\alpha-
 \sqrt{\frac{\left(1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}}.
\]
The left side is nonnegative.  A connected subset of \([-1,1]\) containing both labels has length at least \(2a_\star\).  Consequently
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P[|I_n|]
 \ge E_{Q_{+,n}}[|I_n|]
 \ge2a_\star\left[1-2\alpha-
 \sqrt{\frac{\left(1+\frac{256}{315}\kappa_n^2h_n\right)^n-1}{J_n}}\right]_+.
\]
Taking the infimum over honest rules proves the finite-sample inequality.

It remains to verify the stated limit.  The condition \(T_n=o(\log(1/\kappa_n))\) forces \(\kappa_n\to0\), since otherwise \(T_n=n\kappa_n^{2+1/s}\) diverges at least linearly along a subsequence while \(\log(1/\kappa_n)\) stays bounded.  Thus \(h_n\to0\), and eventually \(h_n\le1/32\).  For such \(n\), since \((16h_n)^{-1}\ge2\),
\[
 J_n\ge\frac1{32h_n}.
\]
Using \(1+x\le e^x\), the chi-square term is bounded by
\[
 \frac{\exp\{(256/315)n\kappa_n^2h_n\}}{J_n}
 \le32h_n\exp\left\{\frac{256}{315}
        \left(\frac{32}{M}\right)^{1/s}T_n\right\}.
\]
Its logarithm is at most
\[
 O(1)-\frac1s\log(1/\kappa_n)
 +\frac{256}{315}\left(\frac{32}{M}\right)^{1/s}T_n,
\]
which tends to \(-\infty\) by the assumed little-oh relation.  The square-root term consequently tends to zero, proving
\[
 \liminf_nL_n(\kappa_n)\ge2a_\star(1-2\alpha).
\]
Finally, the assertion about shrinking oracle intervals is nonvacuous.  For any \(0<\gamma<(2+1/s)^{-1}\), take
\[
 \kappa_n=\rho_n(\log n)^\gamma
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Then \(\rho_n/\kappa_n=(\log n)^{-\gamma}\to0\), so thm:known-cutoff-benchmark gives \(L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\to0\), while
\[
 T_n=(\log n)^{\gamma(2+1/s)}=o(\log(1/\kappa_n)).
\]
This proves the final clause.

open_obligations.what_is_open: A maximal inequality and localization-to-inversion argument with explicit constants for the scan--refine--invert rule, sufficient to prove uniform honesty and the claimed expected-length bound.
open_obligations.obstruction: The current construction names stages of a procedure but does not define a sample map: the grid, contrast weights, thresholds, bias radii, local-polynomial order, and test critical values are unspecified. Different choices change both the localization event and coverage, so the theorem cannot be proved for the named object from the frozen definition.
open_obligations.attempted: The natural bandwidth gives treatment signal-to-noise squared of order T_n and a union bound over translated locations costs order log(1/kappa_n). This recovers the theorem's regime at the level of orders, but it does not certify the particular interval or its uniform constants.
open_obligations.partial_result: At bandwidth \(h_n=(32\kappa_n/M)^{1/s}\), a treatment jump of order \(\kappa_n\) has per-location information of order \(n\kappa_n^2h_n=T_n\), while a grid of disjoint admissible locations has logarithmic size of order \(\log(1/\kappa_n)\).  This verifies the proposed signal-to-entropy scaling.  What is not yet proved is a uniform coverage and length theorem for the named rule because its construction does not specify the dyadic grid, contrast weights, selection thresholds, bias subtraction, local-polynomial order, or the acceptance critical value.

open_obligations.what_is_open: The fixed-level limiting minimax connected expected length and an attaining honest interval throughout the critical window, including the exact transition point.
open_obligations.obstruction: The finite mixture proves a nonshrinking converse only below its explicit signal-to-entropy threshold. Above that threshold its chi-square bound becomes uninformative, while the strong-signal theorem begins only beyond an unspecified constant and itself lacks a completed estimator proof. At the witness threshold, the first-order coordinate lambda alone does not determine the mixture limit because a second-order centering term remains.
open_obligations.attempted: The translated likelihood mixture was evaluated at T_n/log(1/kappa_n) tending to lambda, including the s=1 common-outcome plateau calculation. This yields an explicit one-sided phase constant but neither an effect-label testing lower bound above it nor a matching connected-interval construction.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The explicit witness already evaluates one side of the critical experiment.  Put \(C_h=(32/M)^{1/s}\) and \(C_\psi=256/315\).  Then \(h_n=C_h\kappa_n^{1/s}\), \(\log J_n=s^{-1}\log(1/\kappa_n)+O(1)\), and
\[
 nC_\psi\kappa_n^2h_n=C_\psi C_hT_n.
\]
Thus, along \(T_n/\log(1/\kappa_n)\to\lambda\), the displayed mixture chi-square divergence tends to zero whenever \(C_\psi C_h\lambda<1/s\).  In that subregion the finite-sample argument gives \(\liminf_nL_n(\kappa_n)\ge2a_\star(1-2\alpha)\).  For \(s=1\), the witness threshold is \(\lambda=315M/8192\).  At equality, the first-order coordinate \(\lambda\) does not determine this mixture's limit: the second-order value of \(C_\psi C_hT_n-s^{-1}\log(1/\kappa_n)\) enters.  Above the witness threshold its chi-square divergence grows and the construction supplies no converse.  No honest connected interval with a matched fixed-\(\alpha\) expected-length constant has been constructed in the remaining critical region.
